newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia dlr lurches lower in heavy two-way trade.
newsitem.headline: Australia dlr lurches lower in heavy two-way trade.

text.p: The Australian dollar lurched lower through a brisk morning's trade as offshore sellers swamped support, but did steady somewhat by the midsession

It looked technically unsound from the start after breaching US$0.7790 support overnight but found a moment of relief when the Reserve Bank resisted the temptation to cut rates following its monthly meeting. It was all too brief as a U.S. investment bank sold in size and Swiss and Japanese names joined in, with noteable dumping against the yen, sterling and Canadian dollar.
Enough bids appeared around US$0.7735 to stem the tide, but dealers were bearish and ready to sell again at US$0.7760.
By 12.15 pm (0215 GMT) the local dollar was hovering at US$0.7750/55 after dipping as far as US$0.7736/41 from an early US$0.7764/69 and US$0.7794/99 late here Tuesday.
Traders said a locally-based U.S. investment bank had led the rout overnight and was in the driving seat this morning, forcing the break of US$0.7760 and triggering stop loss slaes.
A number of respected U.S. funds had also lightened positions amid talk of a strategic switch to sterling assets, while Japanese equity houses were serious sellers of AUD/yen.
"When you see some of the big money U.S. names getting out you know its probably time to jump ship," said one dealer.
"The AUD/yen selloff was also a big blow as Tokyo has been a keen buyer recently for dual currency samurai issues," he added.
Traders said the yen was showing a sudden sensitivity to Japanese asset prices in the belief sharp gains in shares and bond yields could presage a tightening in official policy.
Most analysts thought the speculation premature, but it was enough to knock the A$ to 97.24/34 yen by the midsession from 98.07/17 late Tuesday and 99.04/14 the day before.
Sterling, on the other hand, enjoyed the real thing as the new U.K. government sanctioned a 0.25 point rise in official rates and turned over control of policy to the Bank of England.

The hike took U.K. rates to 6.25 percent -- 0.25 point above official rates here -- and the market was already pricing in more, thus giving the pound a healthy interest differential over the A$ on shorter-dated debt.

This in turn drew recommendations from some banks, including SBC, to sell Aussie and buy sterling and there were signs funds had heeded the message. The dollar was down at 0.4736/41 stg from 0.4808/15 late Tuesday.
The weakness on the crosses contributed to a hefty 0.6 point loss on the dollar's trade weighted index leaving it at 60.1 by midday.
Neither could the local currency entirely shake speculation that domestic interest rates were heading lower.

The silence of the RBA today would normally have been taken as a sign a cut was off the agenda for this month, but in this case there was a risk crucial jobs data Thursday would be weak enough to tip the balance.
It was surprise falls in employment for February and March which had first stirred talk of another easing and a further fall in April would put the RBA under intense pressure to cut.
Most analysts, however, expect employment to bounce back by around 35,000 after a 33,900 fall the month before.
A clearer guide to current RBA thinking should emerge tomorrow when governor Ian Macfarlane gives his first testimony on the course of monetary policy to a Parliamentary committee.

The bank's position on policy and assessment of the economy will be released at 10.00 am (0000 GMT) and Macfarlane is expected to actually start speaking from 10.15 onwards and will be answering questions from the committee afterwards.
The testimony could well last past the release of the jobs data at 11.30 am so he may also face questions on the result.
